column1: # The models that .github/scripts/formal.py runs (AUD-5, #389; AUD-6, #409): <name> <files> <what it is> [<slices>], separated by tabs.
# The files are paths below tests/formal, joined in this order into one ProVerif input, which formal.py runs
# with the pinned ProVerif (.github/scripts/formal.py run). The queries of the files are numbered by their
# (* @query id *) comments, and expected.tsv says what each must give in each variant. A line that starts
# A session model is the session of alice with bob, the compromises of one scenario, and the groups of queries that the
# scenario is about: q-reach (the handshake can complete and the server takes the session), q-password (the Login only),
# q-secrecy, q-authserver, q-authclient, q-suite (the sessions, not the control stream), q-negotiation (the control
# stream) and q-replay. Where the attacker holds the Noise key of the server the queries of the client (q-authclient) and
# of replay are left out: there the attacker is the server, and what ProVerif would have to do is to prove a long list of
# attacks false one by one. The scenarios, by what the attacker holds: none; cert (the key of the certificate of the
# server); client (the Noise key of the client); cert-client (both); noise-client (the Noise keys of the server and of
# the client); both (both keys of the server); noise (the Noise key of the server); pw (the password of the user); fs
# precise.pvl, first in a variant, sets preciseActions, so that the prover rebuilds the traces of its attacks (see the file).
# slices: ProVerif keeps its state for every query of a run, so a variant with many queries runs as that many
# ProVerif runs, each with consecutive queries of its own and a job of its own in formal.yml. 1 when the column is
# missing. A variant of this file answers in seconds, but the 34 grades of Noise_IK take about a minute.
# The session with a Login over TLS 1.3 on TCP 443, as the code has it (the vpntest harness runs it; docs/formal-model.md)

column3: TLS-443, pinned certificate, Noise_IK bound to the TLS exporter, the Login with the key pinned: an attacker that is the network
TLS-443: the attacker holds the key of the certificate of the server (the middlebox)
TLS-443: the attacker holds the key of the certificate and the Noise key of the client
TLS-443: the attacker holds the Noise keys of the server and of the client
TLS-443: the attacker holds both keys of the server
TLS-443: the attacker holds every key after the sessions: forward secrecy
TLS-443: the attacker holds the password of the user, whose static key is pinned
TLS-443: the attacker holds the password, and no key is pinned yet (trust on first use)

column1: # The session with a Login over QUIC, as the code has it: the binding is the tls-server-end-point

column3: QUIC, pinned certificate, Noise_IK bound to tls-server-end-point: an attacker that is the network
QUIC: the attacker holds the key of the certificate of the server (finding F1)
QUIC: the attacker holds the Noise keys of the server and of the client
QUIC: the attacker holds every key after the sessions: forward secrecy
QUIC: a client that got no certificate runs an encrypted session, the server a bound one: the handshake cannot complete

column1: # The negative controls: the binding left out, the pin left out, both

column3: Negative control: no binding in the prologue, the attacker holds the key of the certificate
Negative control: the client pins no certificate, the attacker holds the Noise key of the server
Negative control: no pin and no binding, the attacker holds no key: the middlebox

column1: # The control stream of a node to the controller: no password, no record type or suite byte, the node known by its key

column3: Control stream of a C node: the fingerprint of the certificate checked, exporter of the control label: an attacker that is the network
Control stream of a C node: the attacker holds the key of the certificate of the controller
Control stream of a C node: the attacker holds the Noise key of the node, which is all that the controller knows it by
Control stream of a C node: the attacker holds the Noise keys of the controller and of the node
Control stream of a C node: the attacker holds every key after the streams
Control stream of the Go client of Dial, which checks no certificate: an attacker that is the network
Control stream of the Go client of Dial: the attacker holds the Noise key of the controller (finding C1)

column3: Overlay session over TLS-443: the attacker holds the key of the certificate of the server
Overlay session over TLS-443: the attacker holds the Noise key of the dialling node, which is all that the peer knows it by
Overlay session over QUIC: the attacker holds the key of the certificate of the server (finding F1)

Join over TLS-443: the attacker holds the key of the certificate of the server
Join over QUIC: the attacker holds the key of the certificate of the server (finding F1)
